segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back when federal immigration agents launched big operations in North Carolina-- this was back in the middle of November-- one of the things that local reporters did to get a sense of what ICE and Border Patrol were doing-- the scope of it, the kinds of things they were up to-- was that they requested 911 calls.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Charlotte 911. Do you need police, fire, or medic?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: All right. Hold on, please.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When the city releases these to reporters, they altered the voices a little to protect people's identities.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This woman's saying that all morning, these black vans have been showing up at her building, pretending to be exterminators so that people will open their doors. And she thinks they're ICE, and everybody's scared. There have been reports from around the country of immigration agents pretending to be contractors or utility workers or police to trick people and then nab them. And the dispatcher does not know what to do with this.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: OK. So what did you need police assistance with? Did you just want us to know that this is happening in your neighborhood, ma'am?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The woman says, no, she wants the police to come. Because people are intimidated. It's private property. And how is it OK to say they're exterminators when they're not? The picture that you get from these 911 calls-- Ryan Oehrli and Julia Coin collected them for the Charlotte Observer. Jim Daley did it at the Southside Weekly in Chicago. We requested some ourselves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The picture that you get in these calls of immigration officers is different from the videos we've all been seeing online and in the news. The videos capture individual incidents, right? Viral moments. They're often combative or violent. These 911 calls have that sometimes. But they're also something else. Together, they're like a portrait of a country where ICE officers and Border Patrol agents are spreading everywhere, all sorts of run of the mill locations, this new presence that everybody's bumping into. So many of the calls are people who are not targeted by ICE but just calling to say "they're here, getting in the way of daily life."

But they're hovering around and making my guests uncomfortable, along with employees. So I want them off my property. It's my property. And someone needs to inform them of that.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 2
segments.text: Yes, I understand.

segments.speaker: Hotel Caller
segments.text: So they should not be inside of my hotel. They should not be parked at my hotel without any sort of payment. It's my personal property. I'm paying the property taxes for it, not them.

segments.text: Yes, hi. ICE just tear gassed the whole street by Rico Fresh on Armitage and Drake. And I'm a US citizen, and I was just going to a grocery store. And they started tear gassing the whole street. It's ridiculous. Like, are we in a freaking war?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is from Chicago, from when it was flooded with federal agents during Operation Midway Blitz, hundreds of immigration agents all around the city arresting thousands of people.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 3

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It's by Rico Fresh on Armitage and Drake.

segments.speaker: Woman

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In that call, maybe you noticed the dispatcher struggling to figure out exactly what to do for this woman. Does she need an ambulance? She keeps asking. It's unclear in a bunch of these calls what 911 can do to help. And in the calls, you hear both sides, the dispatchers and the callers, as they try to figure it out in real time in this entirely new situation they both find themselves in, where people are calling local police to do something about federal agents.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I should say, for most of these calls, we can verify the basics of what happened through videos or local reporting or other sources. Though there were a handful where all we have is the call, like this next one. A man called 911 with this stumper. He says masked men stopped him and asked him for his ID and violated his rights and damaged his phone. His question for 911 is, next time, if they kidnap me, what do I do?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And if I get kidnapped, what do I do? Who do I call?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 5
segments.text: If you get kidnapped, you can call 911.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 5
segments.text: But you're not currently being kidnapped, correct?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: No, but I could.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 5
segments.text: OK. I hear you.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So basically, if it's just people with masks, then I can defend myself? Can I bring my gun and defend myself?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's a little hard to hear. He's saying, if it's people with masks, can I defend myself? Can I bring my gun and defend myself?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher 5
segments.text: So I can't--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So what is the situation?

segments.text: I can't advise you on anything legal. I'm not an officer or a lawyer. But I can have officers reach out to you and talk more about this.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, please. Do that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, from WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. So here we all are, federal officers shooting American citizens, killing two in Minneapolis. What we hear in these 911 calls is people in real time doing what so many of us are doing, not quite believing what's happening right in front of them, not sure what to do or what can be done, and in this case, calling the place that you're supposed to call when there's an emergency, saying there is one, right here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, we have more of these calls. You'll hear people with 911 on the line as ICE is chasing them, trying to puzzle out their next moves. And you'll hear a bunch of other people trying to outplay armed federal officers in this new version of America that we all find ourselves in. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, What is the Nature of Your Emergency? So before we jump back into more 911 calls, it seems worth saying a word about how we got to this point, that people around the country are calling local law enforcement about the presence of federal law enforcement.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So last year, the Trump administration, hoping to deliver on his campaign promise of mass deportations, it tripled ICE's budget, giving them more money than any federal law enforcement agency. And DHS rapidly hired lots of new enforcement officers-- 12,000, they claim-- more than doubling its workforce.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The Trump administration cut the training time for these new agents in half to 47 days, a number chosen reportedly because Trump is the 47th president. Now they say the training is 42 days. To recruit these agents, DHS ads were all about protecting the homeland and repelling foreign invaders. They used a lot of white nationalist slogans and memes. Google that if you're curious. It's shocking.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And, you know, who knows how many people like that actually signed up? I'm bringing this up because all of that set a certain tone for the agency. This was the new fists out, aggro, coming-for-you branding of our immigration enforcement. And the White House really, really wants them to deliver. The architect of Donald Trump's immigration policy, Stephen Miller, kind of famously berated DHS officials last May and demanded they arrest 3,000 immigrants a day, a quota it is nowhere close to achieving.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So that all sets the stage for the nationwide tour of American cities that federal agents have been on for months, going from one city to the next-- Los Angeles, then Chicago, then Charlotte, then Minneapolis, then New Orleans. Some of the operations got cutesy, trolly names-- Charlotte's Web, Catahoula Crunch, Catch of the Day in Maine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when they arrive in each city, in the calls that I want to play you right now in this act of the show, what's interesting is there are these little runs of calls that tell a story when you listen to them in sequence, one after another after another. It's like you see the immigration agents roll through town on some particular afternoon or evening, moving down the block from corner to corner and spot to spot, leaving a little cloud of chaos each place they touch.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We're going to start with a whole bunch of calls from Charlotte that begin at 10:04 in the morning with a guy who's phoning 911 because ICE seems to be breaking the law. And 911 is the place you call to report somebody breaking the law, right?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Charlotte 911. Do you need police, fire, or medic?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: I just wanted to report we've got a Chevy Tahoe. It's definitely ICE.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: [DISTANT HONKING]

segments.text: They have their license plate-- like, it's covered. I'm pretty sure that that's illegal. It's all covered up. And he's backing into this corner right now.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Oh, he's got a camera out right now. And they're in tactical gear and everything. But it's--

But my concern was the license plate that was deliberately crossed out. And then he's going to want to say that I was following him. But you heard him, how intimidating he was trying to be.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Yeah, that would be great.

segments.text: OK. So that's the first call in this set of calls. 17 minutes later, completely unrelated to that first guy, about a mile and a half away, on the same road, North Tryon Street.

segments.text: The officer's not going to come chase you guys down. In other words, you're on your own.

segments.speaker: Caller

segments.text: This goes on for a little while, the dispatcher asking for a cross street. The guy doesn't know the cross street. And you hear pounding on his windows.

segments.text: A while later, 911 gets this call about the same car in the same location and the guy who was in the car.

segments.text: My cousin had been abducted by ICE, and he's a US citizen. So I need some help on how to proceed. And he is a US citizen. And so what's going on with that? I thought that was just going to be to detain immigrants that are not from here, not also US citizens.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So a man gets pulled from his car. That was one call. Cousin looking for him, that's the next call. And then an hour after that, there's another call about the car that's sitting there, windows smashed in.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: OK. What type of report are you trying to make?

segments.speaker: Caller

But the car is under my name, and he's a cosign, and we're both on the insurance and everything. But I need a police report as far as trying to see what the next steps are.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: All right. I have another call for service. We'll get officers out there as soon as we can.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: An accident report-- that's something the 911 operator knows how to do. The government later filed charges against the guy they pulled from the car. His name is Cristobal Maltos. He's 24. Agents said that when his car moved, he hit an officer with his car mirror, and then charged him with felony assault, resisting, and impeding. A few weeks later, the DOJ dropped the charges.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One thing that hits when you listen to these 911 calls is this feeling like nobody's going to come save you. Superman's not going to show up. The cavalry's not going to come in. The police aren't going to be there. The police aren't going to come because local police won't interfere with federal immigration officers doing their jobs. You hear operators telling that to callers. And you also hear them say, can you just get out of there? Or can you just play along?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For instance, here's another call. We're in the same city, Charlotte, North Carolina, the day after everything you just heard.

And they've been driving recklessly. And they're right on my ass. And I'm a US citizen. I am not immigrated here whatsoever. And they're driving recklessly. They're, like, right on my butt.

segments.text: Keep trying to [INAUDIBLE].

segments.text: OK. Just try to comply as best as you can.

segments.text: I'm putting [INAUDIBLE]

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] I'm on the ground.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It gets kind of faint there. But he's saying, "I'm on the ground. I'm on the ground." This continues for half a minute. Then you hear the dispatcher pipe up again.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Hello? 911

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: [INDISTINCT VOICES]

segments.text: [INDISTINCT SHOUTING AND MUTTERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then there's another half minute or so like this, until, finally--

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: 911 disconnect. I'm getting no response.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: [DISTANT SHOUTING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This happened in the parking lot for a shopping mall. Witnesses heard him yelling, I'm a US citizen, as he was dragged out of the car. Several agents' cars surrounded him. They handcuffed him. They took him. A crowd gathered, upset, filming. The guy's name is Joshua Long. He was detained for six hours, says he was charged with assault on a federal officer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here's something you might not have guessed. It isn't just citizens and immigrants calling in to 911 on these calls. ICE and Border Patrol call too. And they call 911 for a bunch of different reasons. Sometimes it's for the stuff that anybody calls 911. There's one call where federal agents got into a fender bender and wanted to file a regular traffic accident report. Another Border Patrol agent called to report a theft. He said that somebody-- presumably, a protester, but he doesn't say-- broke into his car, stole his work laptop, some ammunition, and his uniform.

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: Let me turned on the lights. I apologize. But I had my badge in there too. I didn't realize that my badge was in there until right now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Calls like these, 911 operators respond to like any other calls. But sometimes ICE and Border Patrol call for help with their jobs out in the field. And that's more complicated. Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, lots of cities, sanctuary cities, don't allow local police to help with immigration arrests. This is a huge bone of contention for the Trump administration, who've tried to sue to change this, and just this week demanded that Minnesota help them as a condition for reducing the number of federal agents there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But one way that some local police do step in-- and step in all the time to help federal agents-- is to manage crowds and protesters who show up around their operations. And in cities where local police are not cooperating with ICE and Border Patrol, one way the federal agents can get them to show up is by calling 911. So, for example, in Worcester, Massachusetts, in May, ICE called repeatedly for police to come to Eureka Street to help them deal with a crowd when ICE arrested a woman as her teenage daughters watched.

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: I need you get there as fast as they can.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: What happened?

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: We have a crowd surrounding an officer, and he's requesting immediate assistance. Can you send units, please?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Was there-- I'm going to send units.

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: Yes, beautiful.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Any weapons that they can tell?

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: Other than the agents? No.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: About how many people is it?

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: About 25.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: 25 people surrounding one officer?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After that, the scene gets pretty unruly. People in the crowd demand to see a warrant for the arrest, though ICE does not need a warrant to arrest somebody. That's something lots of people don't know.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here's one last example of ICE calling 911, in this case, doing something that kind of surprised me to hear so baldly there on a recording. In October, in Oxnard, California. ICE agents deliberately rammed their Jeep Cherokee into the side of a pickup truck of an activist who'd been following them. They T-boned the truck. There's video of this. And then the agents called 911 and lied about what happened.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: 911. What's your emergency?

segments.speaker: Agent
segments.text: Hi. I'm with DHS ICE. I had a local individual crash. They backed into our vehicle. We're pursuing them right now. They're causing a major safety incident. We need locals here now because we're in an active pursuit with the vehicle. He backed into us, and he's fleeing from us. And he's causing an insane safety hazard to this entire area.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ICE hasn't released the name of this agent. He hasn't talked to the press. So we can only guess at why he's saying what he's saying. Maybe he has no idea he was filmed ramming his Jeep into the pickup truck and he's trying to create a record. Maybe he's just saying anything that he thinks would get the local police to come help him. The dispatcher does send police cars out to help. And they stop the pickup. ICE arrests the activist. His name is Leonardo Martinez. But the video of the agents ramming his truck goes viral. He was released a few hours later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Over the eight months since ICE and Border Patrol began these operations around the country, their tactics have gotten more extreme, and the guardrails protecting people's rights have been crumbling. In their first operation in Los Angeles last summer, immigration agents began widespread racial profiling, stopping anybody speaking Spanish or speaking English with an accent. Then in September, the Supreme Court said they would allow that for now. So now they can stop anybody who looks or sounds foreign to them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Another change? DHS issued a new policy saying federal agents could enter somebody's home without a judge's order, which until now was considered unconstitutional. And as things ramped up over this fall, it was made clear to federal agents that if protesters or anybody else tried to slow them down, they could basically do whatever they wanted to them, whatever they saw fit, and they would not be punished. Here's Stephen Miller in October.

segments.speaker: Stephen Miller
segments.text: To all ICE officers, you have federal immunity in the conduct of your duties. And anybody who lays a hand on you or tries to stop you or tries to obstruct you is committing a felony. You have immunity. And no one-- no city official, no state official, no illegal alien, no leftist agitator or domestic insurrectionist-- can prevent you from fulfilling your legal obligations and duties.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So where does that lead? I have one last call I want to play you. It's from Chicago.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Chicago Fire Department. How can I help you?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Can I get medical attention on 36 and California? I've just been shot.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: OK. You said 36th and California?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: 36th and California, please.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: We'll someone right over for you. Where on--

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE]

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: --your body were you shot?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Huh?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Where on your body were you shot?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Huh?

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Where on your body were you shot?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: On my arm and on my leg. Ow. I can't feel my arm no more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Marimar Martinez, a US citizen. She was driving around her neighborhood, warning people that agents were coming, and was shot October 4, three months before Renee Good and Alex Pretti were shot and killed in Minneapolis.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: Help is on the way now. We'll be there shortly. You're outside on the corner there?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: I'm right here in the corner, in the corner, in the corner.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: OK. Help is on the way.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Oh, fucking shit.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: We're going to be there shortly.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Dispatcher
segments.text: We'll meet you there.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Ma'am, do you know who shot you?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Do you have a bandana?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Do you know who shot you, ma'am?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Do you have a bandana? I'm--

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hello, ma'am? Do you know who shot you?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: [INDISTINCT VOICES]

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Oh my god, I feel like I'm going to faint.

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's saying to somebody, do you have a bandana or something to stop this?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Oh, fucking shit.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Please. [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Ma'am, do you know who shot you?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: ICE agents shot me.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Who?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: ICE agents.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: The ICE agent shot you?

segments.speaker: Caller
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Marimar Martinez's case is eerily like Renee Good's. She was in her car, and the government accused her of using her car as a deadly weapon and called her a domestic terrorist. News coverage has documented 13 people who've been shot by immigration agents since these big city sweeps began. And most of them, they were shot in their cars. Also, most of them were accused by federal agents of not complying with orders or trying to escape, or using their car as a weapon.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Two of the people shot in their cars died. The rest survived. This woman, Marimar Martinez, was one of the survivors. In her case, a Border Patrol officer, Charles Exum, said she rammed her SUV into his. She said it was the other way around. And once she got into court on charges that she forcibly assaulted, impeded, and interfered with a federal law enforcement officer, once it got before a judge, the government decided to drop its case.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Martinez's attorney had argued that bodycam evidence clearly showed Exum swerving his vehicle to hit Martinez. Also, it was revealed that Charles Exum, the officer who shot Martinez, bragged about it in texts to his friends, saying things like, "I fired five rounds and she had seven holes. Put that in your book, boys." Before he jumped out of his car and shot her, he was recorded on bodycam footage saying, "do something, bitch." In the end, his glee, his apparent pleasure in the violence of his own actions, turned into a problem for their case and how a jury would see it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In a sense, that's what's happened to these operations nationally. In the last two weeks, their brutality and the seeming incompetence of the people carrying them out, the reckless incompetence, is hard to avoid. It feels like everybody's been talking about it, whatever their politics.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Minnesota, the place that's been ground zero for so much of this lately, the police chief for West Saint Paul, Brian Sturgeon, was asked this week by a resident at a city council meeting, what do we do if ICE agents break the law? Can you help us? In other words, the same question that came up in a few 911 calls. Looking strained and tired, Chief Sturgeon said, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Brian Sturgeon
segments.text: I don't have answers for you on a lot of things. They have a different playbook. They have a playbook that I'm not trained in, our officers aren't trained in. They have a playbook that we disagree with on some aspects of, I'll be honest with you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He seemed truly lost about what he could possibly offer. His suggestion? Call 911.

segments.speaker: Brian Sturgeon
segments.text: I want our citizens to know that if you see something or if-- for instance, if they're hanging-- if they're stopped by a bus stop, call us. We will be there. If you are afraid because they're in the area or they're knocking on your neighbor's house, call us. Know, if you do call 911, we will be there. I know it's not what you want to hear, but yeah, it's a difficult situation. I don't have answers for a lot of the stuff because I don't understand it either.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: President Trump, meanwhile, after first saying this past week that he would be de-escalating immigration enforcement, by the end of the week, said it was going to be full steam ahead. As of today, operations continue in cities around the country.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Chana Joffe-Walt produced that story about 911 calls. Coming up, the glutton of Los Angeles goes to war-- that's in a minute on Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program-- What's Your Emergency? Stories of life in this new America, where federal agents have swept out across American cities. In this half of our show, we're going to turn to people trying to outsmart, outrun, and outplay those forces, beginning now with Act Two. Act two, There's No Place like Home Depot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So there are certain spots around the country getting raided over and over again, like Home Depot parking lots, where day laborers gather looking for work. Back in May, Stephen Miller reportedly yelled at DHS leaders, why aren't you at Home Depot? And then shortly after that, they were, in force.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the very first to get hit in Los Angeles on the first day of the Feds arriving in June was this one in West Lake, LA, on Wilshire Boulevard. And then in August, this same Home Depot was the spot where DHS launched a brand-new strategy that it called Operation Trojan Horse, where Border Patrol agents hid in the back of a Penske truck that pulled up into the parking lot as if it was just a regular moving truck looking to hire people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When workers ran to it to get jobs, the back opened. Agents jumped out in tactical vests with weapons. 16 people were taken that day. And five months later, this same Home Depot is still getting raided. And people are still showing up to find work every day. So what's that like? Months and months of cat and mouse? Reporter Anayansi Diaz-Cortez wanted to find out.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: This Home Depot's not the easiest place to try to conduct a raid. Because at the edge of the parking lot is a kind of safe zone, an area the size of 10 parking spots surrounded by a wrought iron fence. Inside, there's a small building. There's a corrugated roof. Day laborers know, when there's a raid, they can take shelter there.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: It's run by a nonprofit called Carecen, set up years ago to make sure day laborers actually got paid by contractors hiring them. Everyone just calls it El Centro. I want to introduce you to two people who are here just about every day. Daniel Jimenez is a security guard.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: How did you find this job? Yeah. How'd you end up here?

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: My friend's dad is the owner of the security company I'm hired through. Before that, I was a dishwasher at a wedding venue.

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: (SUBJECT) MAN ON RADIO: Gray Dodge coming up to Table 1, Dodge Durango.

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: I didn't know anything about what they did here. I literally just started working here.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Daniel's 20 years old with slouchy younger brother vibes, constantly fidgeting with his vape and often dropping it. Go-to drink at Starbucks across the parking lot-- Mango Dragonfruit Refresher. When you see him at his post just outside the gate to El Centro, he looks bored.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: That's a big contrast with the second person I want to introduce you to, Joshua Erazo, college grad, passionate about nonprofit work and labor policy. That's from his LinkedIn page. His vibe-- softspoken community organizer, the person the day laborers turn to for everything-- job connections, immigration lawyers, coffee, toilet paper, Thanksgiving turkeys. People come to the center for all kinds of stuff, even just to hang out and watch TV. Daniel stands outside the gate. Joshua's inside.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: That's why we have our door system and our locks and all that. But we have the cameras, and I'm ready.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Here's how it works. If there's a raid, workers try to rush inside. Daniel tries to shuttle people through the gate. When they're in, Joshua will lock the gate. It's private property, so federal agents can't enter without a warrant. And it can be pretty harrowing.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: You just hear people screaming, screaming, migra, migra. And then it almost feels like a stampede of people just running to where they can. Holy shit, you know? This is intense.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: One raid in particular stuck with both of them. This was back in August. Immigration agents rolled up with tear gas. People ran towards El Centro. Daniel was outside the gate. Joshua was inside. Daniel thinks he got 15 people in. But then one guy on the way in tripped.

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: He tripped in the middle of the door. And he was just laying there with four ICE agents on him. And I couldn't close the door. And they were trying to get in. So I had to try to close it and not let them get in and not squish him.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: With that guy, it was like, do I save one more and possibly risk everyone, or do I just let them take him? Which is a-- I feel like I stuttered a little bit on that decision for a half a second.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Inside the fence, Joshua was struggling with the same question of when to lock the gate. The immigration agents have now grabbed the man's legs and his shirt. But his shoulder and arm are inside the gate, his hands reaching out for Joshua.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: Kind of reaching out for me to grab him.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Outside the fence, two agents grabbed Daniel and pulled him away from the gate, leaving the door to Joshua alone. Joshua knew the guy stuck in the door, knew him well, said he was like a tio, an uncle, maybe 50 or 60, came around most days.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: And it's like, what do you do? I grab his hand. And all I wanted to do was like, come on in, and close the door. And like, get out of here. And like, yeah, we did it. You were saved. But in the moment, I was thinking to myself, there's people here. There's people over there that the ICE officers can't even see. There's the fact that we have our computers, which might have information. You have to think about all these things. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Joshua makes a quick decision, locks the gate with the man still outside.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: He was at the door. He's a strong dude. He's almost getting away from five other grown men grabbing him. And he's like, Joshua, Joshua, like, Joshua, like that, with his hand out, grunting because he's using his strength, and me having to be-- I can't. I'm sorry. And then the other agents overpowering-- like, throwing him back out the door onto the sidewalk on the floor.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: The guy's shirt had almost been completely ripped off by the officers. Joshua watched from behind the locked door as they arrested him. He says the rest of the day, he kept asking people, did I do the right thing? What would you have done?

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: I just felt like shit. I felt like I failed him. I felt like to see someone taken in front of you with their hand out and you, in essence, being like, no, I'm not going to grab your hand, it kind of feels like I let them down. But then you think about, what if I had done that? Like, they would have opened the door, and they would have came in.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: But then it's like, fuck, if it went the other way, maybe 12 people had gotten taken, you know? I think I was asking the others just to be like, well, what would you have done? Would you have grabbed their hand? Would you not have grabbed their hand? I guess trying to affirm that I made-- not the best decision, but I made the decision that had the least amount of negative consequences.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: I have this thing that keeps coming to mind when you're talking about this.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: This is my producer, Lilly Sullivan.

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Have you ever heard of this-- I think it's an ethical situation. Like, if a train is going down the tracks and you're the conductor and there's one person on one track or six people on the other--

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: Who would you save?

segments.speaker: Lilly Sullivan
segments.text: Yeah. And you lived that situation. Like, it's actually that situation. And you were the conductor.

segments.speaker: Joshua Erazo
segments.text: Yeah. I would just blow up the train so it couldn't get to either one, the train being here ICE. But no, I wouldn't inflict any violence on anybody. But my solution would be remove the train from the equation so that people can live.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: There's one more operation I want to tell you about that felt big for a different reason. This one happened just a few weeks ago while I was in the Starbucks there in the parking lot. A woman opened the door and shouted, "ICE is here. [SPANISH] ICE." Baristas froze, panicked. Drinks started flying. I left my drink on the counter and rushed out.

segments.speaker: Volunteer
segments.text: [SHOUTING IN SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Volunteer
segments.text: White Tahoe! The white Tahoe is ICE. The white Tahoe running down Union Avenue is ICE!

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: I head for El Centro. I expected outside to be chaos. But what happened instead, it was creepily still.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Oh my god, the whole front is empty. There's no more workers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Everyone just left. The SUVs circle.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: They're coming up. They're coming back.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: They're coming back.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: But then it's just the screeching of tires. As far as I can tell, no one gets taken from the parking lot. This round, the immigration agents just left. The center was locked down. Inside, some workers watched a Jean-Claude Van Damme movie.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: The hero, the one who sounded the alarm, the one who spotted ICE-- I honestly didn't see this coming. It was Daniel, the 20-year-old who stands outside the gate. He spotted them first. He was on high alert, pacing. For months now, he'd been memorizing license plates every day from photos a community watch group had sent around.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: What'd you see?

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: It was two Ford Expeditions. Would you like the plates?

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Daniel Jimenez
segments.text: There was a California paper plate, BTC1984, and then a Texas plate, WNJ3422.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: He told me he'd started memorizing them because checking his phone was too slow. That other raid weighed on him, the day he said he stuttered. He didn't want to stutter again.

segments.speaker: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez
segments.text: I think lots of people right now are finding themselves in roles they did not see coming, doing things they never imagined. One of the bosses here has a new nickname for Daniel. He calls him El Monstruo de la Puerta, the monster of the door, which is new. This didn't used to be a place that needed a monster at the door.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Anayansi Diaz-Cortez. Lilly Sullivan produced that story.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Memo to the Future. "Emergency" suggests something immediate and short term that happens fast, runs on adrenaline, and then ends. Miki Meek has this story about a guy who's been in emergency mode for eight months now.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Los Angeles was way ahead of Minnesota's governor, Tim Walz, when he called on people to carry their phones on them at all times to record immigration raids. LA's been making videos all along. The hard part is keeping track.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Did you get that one, Izzy?

segments.speaker: Izzy Ramirez
segments.text: Which one?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: In Glendale, Vine and Columbus.

segments.speaker: Izzy Ramirez
segments.text: Vine and Columbus?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Yeah, that's a new one.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo Torres and Izzy Ramirez are building an archive, every day's raids, arrests, sightings of federal agents in Southern California, 230 days and counting. Memo delivers a roundup at the end of every day, just him, speaking to the camera and playing video clips. It's called The Daily Memo.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: It's Monday, August 11, and it's day 67 of the ICE siege of LA.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: It's Wednesday, October 15, and it's day 133.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Today's Thursday, November 20, and it's day 168. A mother ran with her infant as her husband was taken by agents. We confirmed about 14 people kidnapped by masked federal agents today from--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I don't even live in Los Angeles. And yet, I've been watching The Daily Memo for months. It speaks to something about this moment. For a while now, almost every day has felt like, I can't believe this day happened. And also, what did happen, exactly? The Daily Memo is trying to organize that chaos.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo records the Daily Memo video at night. And then during the day, all day, almost every day for months now, he and Izzy are in the small room in LA, a work studio, sitting in front of computers while their phones are blowing up with texts and DMs and videos from around the city.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Look over all the footage. Is the footage uploaded?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo's got two screens in front of him. When I was there, one screen was a map zoomed in on Northeast Los Angeles, with pins where that day's raids had happened so far.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: You done with the doc, Izzy, or you still updating?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The other screen had a Google Doc with bullet points and links to videos that he and Izzy were making together. They cross-check videos, call witnesses, often community watch teams and rapid responders. They're weeding out fake or mislabeled videos. In the room, it's long silences and then quick shorthand as they try to gather, verify, and archive the same bundle of information for each incident in each day. Like how many people taken--

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Yesterday was 14.

segments.speaker: Izzy Ramirez
segments.text: Yeah. And then the day before that, I had-- so that's 28 plus 8. That's 36, 36 people.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: What time--

segments.speaker: Izzy Ramirez
segments.text: Do you know what time the Classic Car Wash was?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: What time the what?

segments.speaker: Izzy Ramirez
segments.text: The Classic Car Wash, not City Car Wash?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And where--

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: And here's this one saying that ICE is in Inglewood.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It is a total grind, both monotonous and distressing. Memo is 6 foot 4. And he's got this big beard, perfect hair. The first time I met him, he was taking his first day off work in six months.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Do you have a threshold for yourself of being like, I will do this until X? I'll do this until I know I gotta do something else?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Yeah, it's interesting. I don't have too much time to think about all that, to honest with you. I'm literally living in, minute by minute, to what's happening with ICE. People are like, oh, Memo, we don't want you to burn out. I'm like, I burn out every fucking day. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: You know? I go home. And then I crash and then eat an edible, put on some TV, go and pass out, and then wake up the next day and just be like, fuck, here we go again. But it's no different from my landscaping and gardening days, where it was just the same grind every single day.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Yeah. What are the things that are useful from that life for this one?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Just fucking shut up and work. Nothing about that life, the day laborer life or the gardening life, is pleasant-- nothing about it. You're dealing with people that are passively racist, hard-ass work. Even in the worst of weather, whether it be hot and dry or cold, freezing, and miserable, you still gotta get out there and mow the lawns, trim the trees, trim the bushes, dig the ditches, get dirty, back pains, sores.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: And when you wake up the next day, it doesn't matter how bad your body feels or how tired your mind is. You get right back up, 5:30, meet the crew, get your coffee and your donut, and get right back to it. So all of that, I brought with me. So it's like, yeah. So what, it was tough? Yesterday, it was tough. Today, it's going to be tough again. And tomorrow's going to be tough again. And that's the routine of life.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo is 45 years old, Mexican-American. He's lived his whole life in LA. He had his own landscaping business for 16 years and then, almost a year ago, managed to turn the thing he did for fun into his job. He liked to photograph and post about the places he ate at on his lunch breaks-- taco trucks, little burrito hole in the walls, taqueros who'd set up shop on sidewalks.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: His Instagram handle was @el_tragon_de_los_angeles, the Glutton from Los Angeles. And a website called LA Taco hired him full time. He did food reviews for them, like The Giant Taco Hiding Under the 10 Freeway. But within a few months, federal agents showed up in the city, and Memo and the rest of the staff at LA Taco switched to covering raids and protests. There wasn't even a big discussion about it. It just made sense. The people they all regularly saw and talked to were now targets.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So the whole organization changed overnight from being a membership-based website with local food and culture stories, with some news, to still being that, plus a home for The Daily Memo. One of the top metro reporters for the LA Times says no one else in the city, including the LA Times, is doing this kind of detailed daily accounting. This record Memo started? This is it.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo had a specific audience in mind when he started. The Daily Memo is in English, partly because he was trying to reach the younger, more online members of Latino families in LA, the ones taking care of paperwork and bureaucracy, the kids of street vendors, gardeners, day laborers, the ones now trying to keep their parents safe.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: In The Daily Memo, he would tell the audience what parts of the city and surrounding areas are getting hit, what times of day. And when he saw patterns and trends emerging in the videos, he'd point them out. Every Daily Memo, by the way, starts out with a cartoon taco on the screen and the sound of a bite being taken out.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: [BITE CRUNCHES]

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Today is Thursday, November 6, day 154 of the ICE siege. Most of today's abductions happened on the streets, including questioning a homeless man. They also raided a U-Haul on Jeronimo and El Toro, which seems to be a new target of theirs, like they just learned that they also have day laborers. Well, they took four people from that U-Haul. Another new favorite target-- recycling centers. They flooded--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo and Izzy get videos and tips no one else does because they're not outsiders. They're trusted. Memo was one of the first to track what places were getting raided again and again-- car washes, school dropoff areas, Home Depots. He knows who they often targeted-- Latinos in work clothes, a lot of older people, 50 plus.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The Daily Memo tracked the evolution of immigration raids in LA from a hodgepodge of random agents, often in street clothes and with no visible identification, to a more consistent, militarized look-- green Border Patrol vests, sometimes helmets with rifles. Over time, there are more videos of agents opening fire on people. The first US citizens arrested in Los Angeles were big stories. Now those are common, in LA and elsewhere.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: When DHS accuses people of assaulting federal agents, The Daily Memo is a place lawyers go to look for videos that may prove them wrong. And there's one more kind of video in The Daily Memo's archive, these eerie still lifews-- a food cart with meat still sizzling on the grill, but no one's there. A row of buckets with bouquets in them. A lunch bag left in front of an apartment complex. The aftermath of someone being taken.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Memo showed me a video of a woman stumbling on a gardening truck on a residential street, no one in it or nearby. The open truck bed is full of tools and gear.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: So we're in Ribidoux, right off of Mission Avenue and Crestmore.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: They got rakes, lawnmowers, blowers, shovels, ladders, pipes.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So in that instance, what are you doing?

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: Well, we'll just report that we found an abandoned truck. Because a lot of people find out about this stuff through the videos. They'll comment, that was my cousin. That was my dad. Oh my god, we were wondering where he was at. And they'll reach out through the DMs. And then I get to talk to them and be like, OK, I'm sorry. That's how we verify that it was actually an ICE agent.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: I learned two of my former employees, when I had my landscape company, that were deported from some of these videos. I'm like, dude, these are people that I worked with for, like, 15 years. I know them really well. I know their families.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: At the end of the night, after Memo finished recording The Daily Memo, I sat next to him and pulled up some old black-and-white photos on my phone from the 1950s of Mexican men in work hats lined up to board planes and trains. This is when the government ran another big deportation campaign in California targeting Mexican immigrants and named it after a slur-- Operation Wetback. And looking at them, one thing really stood out to Memo.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: There are no chains or shackles. There's no military gear. There's no rifles. Look, it's like Barney Fife right there, right?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Barney Fife, the bumbling sheriff from The Andy Griffith Show.

segments.speaker: Memo Torres
segments.text: I wasn't there, and I won't say that the cruelness wasn't there. But you don't see the cruelness in the images then as you're seeing it now.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: How will these videos look in 5 years, 20 years, 50? What are we going to think about them? Memo's got his mind on the future too. He and Izzy are downloading all the videos so they can't disappear. At some point, in some future America, maybe they'll lead to a reckoning.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Miki Meek is a producer on our show.
